cards.title: Plain-Language Rewrite of Product Copy
cards.summary: Strip school-taught 'big words' from product descriptions and ad copy so shoppers instantly understand what you sell.
cards.use_when: Rewriting a product page, category description, paid-ad copy or email when traffic bounces or copy reads like a corporate brochure.
steps: Scan the draft for inflated substitutes: 'enervated' for tired, 'famished' for hungry, 'elephantine' for big, 'recalcitrant' for stubborn, 'nefarious' for evil. Replace each with the everyday word.
Delete formal filler phrases the source calls out: 'and you'll enjoy same', 'the aforementioned benefits', 'you can liken this to', 'herein are 10 reasons'.
For each product-page bullet, read it aloud to a non-specialist; if they hesitate, cut or replace the word.
Ask whether the sentence tells the shopper what she gets, not how clever the writer is. The source argues copy has one job: to sell.
Apply the simplification to every asset you reuse (ad, PDP, landing page, email) because the trained habit follows you into every format.
Where a genuinely technical term is necessary for a niche audience (e.g., specs for pro buyers), keep it but define it in the same sentence.
caveats: The source's claim that unclear words 'flush money down the toilet' is opinionated; there is no measured conversion number attached.
Technical or expert audiences may expect precise terminology — simplify the surrounding sentence, not the term itself.

cards.title: Short Sentences, Short Words, Short Paragraphs
cards.summary: Use one idea per sentence, ~11 words on average, and mostly one-syllable words to keep readers moving through sales copy.
cards.use_when: Formatting the body copy of a product landing page, sales email or catalog ad where you need prospects to read every selling point.
steps: Apply Flesch's targets as quoted by the source: about 70–80% of words should be one syllable, and sentences should average roughly 11 words.
Enforce the rule of one thought per sentence; put the next point in the next sentence rather than joining with 'and' or 'but'.
Keep regular paragraphs to about four or five short sentences so the page doesn't read as a wall of text.

Use the short-paragraph trick sparingly: pose a question or one-line statement, then answer or continue in the next paragraph in a few words (e.g., 'Would you like to know a secret way to make money watching TV? / I thought so. / Now let me explain...').
Check that opening sentences of the body are deliberately tiny — the source notes copywriter Drew Kaplan often opens paragraphs with two-to-four-word sentences like 'I confess.' or 'It's tough.'
Don't overdo the trick — the source warns mechanical-looking copy loses the effect.
caveats: Ogilvy's 'max 11 words in your opening paragraph' and the 70–80% one-syllable target are the source's cited heuristics, not tested conversion guarantees.
Repeating the two-to-four word pattern in every paragraph reads as gimmick; vary it.

cards.title: Personal Pronoun Density for Warm Copy
cards.summary: Load headlines and body copy with 'you' and 'I' to turn mass advertising into personal communication.
cards.use_when: Drafting headlines, product descriptions or email subject lines that currently sound distant and corporate.
steps: Sprinkle 'you' and 'I' throughout every asset — the source says it is nearly impossible to overuse 'you' in well-written copy.
Start or end sentences with 'you': 'Do you…', 'Can you…', 'Would you…', 'Should you…'.
Write question prompts the source lists: 'May I ask you a question? May I ask your advice? Can I get your opinion? Did you know… Let me tell you… I think you'll like this idea…'.
Put 'you' in the headline itself, not just the body — the headline is where most skimmers stop.
Apply this to onboarding and retention emails too: framing the message as a one-to-one note raises its perceived relevance.
caveats: The source's claim that pronoun-heavy copy is 'the most effective kind' is an advertising convention, not a quantified result.

cards.title: Feature-to-Benefit 'Big Deal' Translation
cards.summary: Convert every product spec into a WIIFM benefit by forcing each feature through the 'You benefit by…' test.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP bullets, bundle descriptions or ad copy from a spec sheet that currently lists only features.
steps: List each feature as a plain component (e.g., 'multiple ink tanks', '500-sheet tray', 'ultra-draft mode button').

For each, mentally shout 'BIG DEAL! What's in it for me?' then complete the sentence 'You benefit by…'. Example: multiple ink tanks → 'You benefit by saving money because you don't replace the whole cartridge when one color runs out.'
Keep the buyer's reaction as the copy — the source's printer example shows the prospect immediately self-identifies with the pain ('I spend a fortune for ink with my current printer').

Use the source's Rolls-Royce examples as the pattern: hand-selected leather → luxurious comfort in all climates; deep-pile wool carpeting → rich softness underfoot; 453-hp V-12 → power, control, supreme reliability; Spirit of Ecstasy hood ornament → feeling of power and 'arrived' status.
Run the same drill on every bundle or upsell item so cross-sell copy names the gain, not the components.
Strip anniversary notices, staff photos and company milestones unless they come with a price cut or buyer gain.
caveats: The feature/benefit split is the source's framing; a benefit that isn't credible becomes hype.
Do not convert a benefit into an unsupported numeric promise (e.g., 'save 50% on ink') unless your own product data supports it.

cards.title: Biggest Benefit in the Headline
cards.summary: Put the single most important buyer benefit in the headline so 60% who only skim headlines still get the selling message.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising headlines for paid ads, emails, product pages or category banners.
steps: Write down the #1 reason a shopper would buy; that becomes the headline, not a brand name or vague claim.

Replace amorphous claims. The source's before/after: 'Louise Taylor Designs Homes of Distinction' → 'Award-Winning Interior Designer Louise Taylor Turns Your House Into a Gorgeous Model Home for Less than You Ever Dreamed Possible!'
Select the audience in the headline itself. The source contrasts 'We'll Help You Brighten Up Your Life and Save Big!' with the simple 'Need Lamps?' — the audience is instantly flagged.

Use the concrete-offer pattern when running a promotion: 'GIANT FILM SALE! All Rolls of 35mm Color Film are 25% Off—This Week Only!' or 'Attention Chocolate Lovers: Now Sink Your Teeth Into the 8½-Pound Fudge-Devil Volcano Pie—Absolutely Free!'.
Give the specific payoff over the 'tricks of the trade' framing: 'New Workshop Teaches You How to Boost Your Tips by 512%…or Your Money Back!' — though back claims you can substantiate.
caveats: The 60% headline-and-nothing-else and 3,000-exposure figures are the source's cited estimates; treat as directional.
Ogilvy's 'unless your headline sells, you wasted 90% of your money' is the source's quotation of an opinion, not a measured result.

cards.title: Short vs. Long Headline Trade-off
cards.summary: Shorter headlines are read more, but readability does not guarantee effectiveness — benefit outweighs brevity.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a compact and a long, information-heavy headline for an ad, email subject line or PDP hero.
steps: Follow the source's two-rule priority: (1) always put the biggest benefit in the headline; (2) where two headlines are equally effective, the shorter one is read by more people.

Reference the source's cited readership bands by headline length: up to 3 words 87.3%; 4–6 words 86.3%; 7–9 words 84%; 10–12 words 82.5%; 13+ words 77.9%. Readership drops most sharply above 12 words.
Keep in mind the source's cognitive basis: people process roughly five to nine items in one act of attention, and grasp about five to six words in a single glance.
Accept occasional long headlines — the source notes well-written long headlines that flow into subheads can be remarkably effective in direct-response ads.
Do not chop a headline so short it loses audience selection or the benefit — the source states a short headline is not automatically an effective one.
caveats: Readership bands come from the source's cited 1939–40 Saturday Evening Post study and Starch research — dated figures, treat as directional.
Ogilvy and the source disagree on long vs. short: Ogilvy said longer headlines sell more. Choose per context.

cards.title: 22 Tested Headline Starters
cards.summary: Use a bank of proven opening words to set the tone of a headline while swapping in your specific product, offer and benefit.
cards.use_when: Stuck drafting headlines for a new product launch, promotion, category page or email campaign.
steps: Pick a starter word from the source's 22 and swap in your product: FREE, NEW, AT LAST, THIS, ANNOUNCING, WARNING!, JUST RELEASED, NOW, HERE'S, THESE, WHICH OF, FINALLY, LOOK, PRESENTING, INTRODUCING, HOW, AMAZING, DO YOU, WOULD YOU, CAN YOU, IF YOU, STARTING TODAY.
Match the starter to the buyer's awareness: 'Announcing' and 'Introducing' for launches; 'Warning!' for problem-solving offers; 'How' and 'Do you' for instructional angles.

Follow the patterned examples — 'How to Sing Like an American Idol in 90 Days or Less—Guaranteed'; 'If You Hate Cleaning Your Pool, This Ad Brings Good News!'; 'Would You Trade $2 for Our Famous Brick-Oven Pizza?'.
Anchor most headlines to John Caples' four qualities: self-interest, news, curiosity, and quick/easy way — self-interest and news usually carry the load.
Test multiple starters for the same product rather than committing to one, and check they still select a qualified audience.
caveats: The source warns against cute or clever headlines that don't target the right audience ('SEX!' for patio furniture) — the goal is the right eyeballs, not all eyeballs.
Free, guarantee and time-bound claims must match your actual offer and local advertising rules.

cards.title: 12 Openers That Bridge Headline to Body Copy
cards.summary: Pull the reader from the headline into the sales copy using one of 12 proven opening devices.
cards.use_when: The headline works but the body copy starts flat on a landing page, sales email or catalog ad.
steps: Choose a device and align it with the headline's promise: continue the thought; ask a question; quote a respected authority; give a free taste; challenge the reader to prove it works; start with a story of skepticism.

Add bandwagon, reporter, and personal-address options: tell what others are saying with a signed testimonial; write as a reporter ('Philadelphia, PA—A New York psychologist has just released the findings of a seven-year study…'); open directly with 'you' questions.

Use dramatic-story or super-detailed spec openers when the product story is emotional or technical — e.g., detailing an '8½ × 11-inch leatherbound, hardcover' book with 'over 327 pages, 10 information-filled chapters, and 45 of the most effective new communication tools'.
Try a very short first sentence to lure readers in: 'Don't you hate it?', 'It's so annoying!', 'I can't stand it!'.
Apply the 'free taste' opener on PDPs by giving one usable tip or sample step before the ask — the source shows it works in print.
caveats: Quoting an authority or publishing testimonials requires real, attributable sources — the source's examples are illustrative.
Super-detailed specs need accurate figures; guessing damages credibility on a PDP.

cards.title: Break the Rectangle: Shape and Scroll-Stopping Design
cards.summary: Use shape difference — circular ads over the dominant square/rectangle — to stand out from competing placements.
cards.use_when: Placing display ads in a feed, marketplace or newsletter where your creative will sit cluttered among competitors.
steps: Acknowledge the source's observation that most print ads are square or rectangle simply because publishers optimize their sales space, not because square outperforms.
Ask the designer or printer to set the ad inside a circular border within the standard square space you buy; keep the copy layout normal rather than curving text around the interior.
Fill the area between the outer edge of the circle and inner edge of the square with a solid color (often black) so the circle is emphasized.
Give the horizontal-center area the most copy: a circle naturally offers more width at the middle than at top and bottom.
For ecommerce placements, translate the principle as stand-out creative in cluttered environments (distinctive shape or framing in a display slot) — not as a literal circle on a mobile feed.
caveats: The source's supporting evidence is Printer's Ink from decades ago in print — treat as directional, not a universal conversion result.
Ad platforms often control creative shape; test distinctiveness within the allowed format.

cards.title: Never Reverse Long Body Type
cards.summary: White (or light) type on a dark background cuts legibility and slows reading — reserve it for short, large headlines.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a website, email or ad creative with dark backgrounds behind text.
steps: Check every text element: if body copy is lighter than its background, flip it to dark type on a light background.

Apply the source's cited evidence: G. Holmes (1931) found black-on-white text legible at ~66 inches versus ~55 inches for reversed; Daniel Starch measured a non-reversed reading speed just over six words per second versus just over four for reversed.
Note Paterson and Tinker's results: reversed passages read 4% less legibly when compared immediately after a normal passage, and 16% less legibly when participants read only reversed copy.
Keep the exception: reverse large headline type with few words out of a solid dark background (e.g., 'Free Chocolate Truffles!').
On a website, avoid dark hero sections with long light-grey paragraph copy; use a light card or overlay for body text.
caveats: Evidence is the source's citation of 1930s–1940s studies; more recent screen research may differ.
Dark mode interfaces are common and expected by many users — the principle applies to long-form sales copy, not necessarily UI text.

cards.title: Extreme Specificity: Educate the Shopper With Detail
cards.summary: Describe your product's process, materials and numbers in exhaustive specifics so your listing feels more substantial than generic competitors.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, brand story or category copy where competitors all use the same vague 'quality ingredients' language.
steps: List what you do that is invisible to the market — sourcing, process, preparation, craftsmanship, guarantees — and put it in the copy.

Contrast the source's two pizzerias: Luigi's ('wonderful home cooking' plus a coupon) versus Fratelli's, which specified fresh bread baked daily, from-scratch pasta, fresh herbs, pure cold-pressed virgin olive oil, spring water, Italian music, softly glowing candles.

Contrast the two hardware stores: the first listed categories at 'neighborhood-friendly prices'; Handyman Jack's cited 343 kinds of fasteners, 28 types of nails, 86 gauges of wire, 43 grit sizes of sandpaper, 16 hammer styles, 47 types of keys, 354,000 daily bolts and screws, top-name tools for less, and a no-nonsense money-back guarantee.
Use numerical specifics where they're honest: counts of SKUs, finishes, sizes, years of family craft (the source's four-generation, 80-year example).
Include sensory detail, not just data — 'golden and crusty bread', 'chewy interior crust' — to help shoppers pre-experience the product.
Understand the mechanism the source names: Length-Implies-Strength — because few competitors say these things, the one who does reads as bigger, more complete, more successful.
caveats: The source acknowledges some details are objectively trivial — the effect comes from the psychology of detail, not necessity.
Every count, source claim and guarantee must be true and verifiable or you risk consumer-protection exposure.
Unconfirmed adjectives like 'award-winning' should only accompany an actual award.

cards.title: Ogilvy Two-Thirds Layout and Caption Rule
cards.summary: Structure ads and hero sections with a dominant visual, headline below it, and copy beneath — plus a selling caption under every image.
cards.use_when: Designing a display ad, print insert or a PDP/landing-page hero where the image-to-copy balance needs a proven arrangement.
steps: Use the Two-Thirds/One-Third (the 'Ogilvy') layout: top two thirds is one large photograph; headline directly beneath it; body copy below; company logo in the lower-right corner.
Or use the Reverse Ogilvy: photo on top third, headline beneath it, remaining two thirds sales copy, logo lower-right.
Start body copy with a drop cap — the source cites Ogilvy's claim of a 13% average readership increase.
Treat the headline and body copy as the photo's caption; the eye moves to the image first, then down.

Put a caption under every illustration — the source cites evidence that up to twice as many people read captions as body copy, and both Ogilvy and John Caples instructed copywriters to write selling captions.
caveats: Layout evidence is adapted from print research (Starch and Ogilvy); screen behavior and mobile layouts may differ.
The 13% drop-cap figure is attributed by the source to Ogilvy, not reinterpreted as a general benchmark.

cards.title: Typeface Choice for Ease of Reading
cards.summary: Choose readable faces — serif for printed body text, initial caps for headlines — to prevent large chunks of readers abandoning copy.
cards.use_when: Specifying fonts for a catalog, print flyer, packaging, or the body text of a website or landing page.
steps: Use a serif face for body copy on paper: the source cites Wheildon's tests showing 66% comprehension for Garamond, versus less than 50% for Times Roman and 12.5% for Helvetica in one several-hundred-thousand-reader test.

Avoid excessively decorative fonts; the source singles out Flag Day-style, letter-obscuring faces as nearly unreadable, and notes research showing Cloister Black slowed reading by 16.5% and American Typewriter by 5.1%.

Choose from serif faces commonly recommended by practitioners the source names — Adobe Caslon, Adobe Garamond, ITC Stone Serif, Janson Text 55 Roman, Baskerville, Cheltenham Bold for headlines, Century, Caslon, Jenson, Courier for sales letters, Schoolbook for body.

Set headlines longer than a couple of words in initial caps rather than all caps: the source cites Paterson and Tinker's 11.8% readership drop for all caps, and a further test finding an 18.9% gap favoring initial caps.
Understand the mechanism for the caps rule — the eye recognizes words by outline, and all caps removes the ascender/descender variation that distinguishes words.
caveats: The serif/sans-serif comprehension figures are 1980s print studies from the source; screen rendering and resolution differ, and sans-serif is standard for digital UI.
The source itself notes no definitive study picking a single best serif; the practitioner preferences are opinions.
Comprehension percentages are source-cited findings, not conversion benchmarks.

cards.title: Deadlines and Scarcity to Beat Buyer Inertia
cards.summary: Add a hard or soft deadline to every offer so prospects act while the salesperson is still in front of them.
cards.use_when: Finalizing a promotion, launch, restock or cart-abandon email where the CTA currently has no reason to act now.
steps: Decide between a hard deadline with a specific cut-off ('Sale Ends August 21st') or a soft deadline ('Quantities are Strictly Limited').

Use the source's standard phrases: 'Call Before April 5th', 'Supplies Are Strictly Limited', 'Offer Expires May 15', 'Price Guaranteed Only Until August 3', 'Offer Good Only Before 4 p.m.', 'Seating Is Limited to 50 Participants', 'NO Rain Checks Will Be Issued', 'Good Only for the First 50 Callers'.
Translate for ecommerce: countdown to end of sale, low-stock indicators, limited-run quantities, member-only windows, expiry on the discount code.

Apply the underlying psychology the source cites — Cialdini's scarcity weapon, where fear of loss gives deadlines their power — and note the source frames this as acting when the offer is presented, not just asking for the order.
Put the deadline in the headline, above the CTA and in the reminder email sequence.
caveats: A soft deadline like 'limited stock' must reflect real inventory constraints or it becomes a trust problem.
Fake countdown timers and always-on 'flash sales' can dilute the mechanism and trigger consumer-protection complaints in some jurisdictions.

cards.title: Repeating 'You Learned' to Escalate Credibility
cards.summary: Use repeated paragraph leaders that echo the promise to speed reading, add tempo and imply volume of proof.
cards.use_when: Writing sales-page, webinar-recap or follow-up email copy where you need to consolidate the argument and drive the reader onward.
steps: Start consecutive paragraphs with the same leader phrase so the reader's eye is pulled down the page: 'YOU LEARNED…', 'We Guarantee…', 'We Promise…', 'You'll Receive…'.
In each follow-on paragraph, restate one point the reader has already been shown — the source's example repeats 'YOU LEARNED' across five paragraphs summarizing earlier lessons.
Alternate with benefit restatements so the repetition isn't pure self-congratulation — each leader should reintroduce a benefit or promise.
Use the technique at the summary page of a long PDP, in email sequences recapping earlier content, or on the post-purchase page to reanchor the value of the purchase.

Accept the source's rationale: the repetition increases perceived volume, and the source argues it can cause skeptical readers to doubt their own resistance because the copy sounds confident, specific and repeated.
caveats: The source acknowledges the reader may not actually have learned all the points being repeated — this is a persuasion technique, not an informational one.
Overusing paragraph leaders makes copy feel mechanical and can erode trust.

This is especially unfortunate when the person writes advertising! But there’s a good reason why people write that way: that’s how many people were taught to write! In school, we were taught to write as adults. To talk with “big” words. So the word tired became enervated. Hungry became famished. Big became elephantine. Stubborn became recalcitrant. Evil became nefarious. Sigh...you get the idea. But do you see what has happened to you and me? Because we were trained to write this way, we tend to write this way whenever we write anything. This means that every time we write an ad, brochure, sales letter, e-mail, or Web page, we are, in effect, flushing our money down the toilet. Why? Because nobody understands what the $@#!* we’re talking about! Forget those annoying $10 words and phrases you were taught in school and business. You know the ones I mean: and you’ll enjoy same, the aforementioned benefits, you can liken this to, herein are 10 reasons, and any other of those tired, stodgy expressions. Just be clear, natural, and simple.

 Ad-Agency Secrets 87 Prescription #2: The Shorter Your Sentences, the Better It’s easier to read short sentences, isn’t it? Sure is! It’s quick! Lively! Exciting, too, wouldn’t you say? Chop your sentences down with a big ol’ ax. You’ll rivet people’s eyes to your sales copy, encouraging them to read more. Rule of thumb: Express only one thought in a sentence, no more. Use your next sentence to say the next thing. Why? Because it’s much easier for your readers to process and understand just one thought at a time. And because everything you say is important, you want them to understand each of your sales points, don’t you? Of course. So do as the good Dr. Flesch suggests: (1) Use shorter words—70 to 80 percent of them should consist of just one syllable, and (2) write shorter sentences—aim for about 11 words each. People will read more. The more they read, the greater your chance of persuading them to buy. The more they buy, the more money you make. Any questions? Prescription #3: The Short, Short Paragraph Trick Here’s a great trick used by today’s top copywriters to keep people reading and moving ahead at a quick pace. You simply ask a question or make a quick statement, and then answer the question or continue the thought in the next paragraph in just a few words. Here’s an example. Dear Bob, Would you like to know a secret way of making money by simply watching TV? I thought so. Now let me explain... Not only does this short-paragraph trick move your readers’ eyes down the page, but it also quickens their pace and makes your ad or letter look much more inviting. (As opposed to a big, solid page full of text.) Don’t overdo this technique, or your writing will look too mechanical. Limit your regular paragraphs to about four or five short sentences. Drew Alan Kaplan knows this trick well. In his wildly popular directmail catalog of high-tech electronic gadgets, Kaplan writes extremely engaging copy that sells products like hotcakes. He took a tiny business CA$HVERTISING 88 run from his cramped dorm room at UCLA, and grew it into a slamming 400-person sales machine that moved, for example, 450,000 radar detectors, 250,000 stereo equalizers, 100,000 subwoofers, and 900,000 bread makers. (Yours truly bought a radar detector, and I’m still baking fresh bread today. Yep, I’m a sucker for great copy.) In virtually every one of his full-page catalog ads, he starts the first paragraph with sentences consisting of only two to four words. Of the eight products I just now reviewed on his Website, six of them use this technique: ✸ “I confess.” ✸ “We’re free.” ✸ “It’s tough.” ✸ “This is important.” ✸ “S.W.A.T. teams use them.” ✸ “It’s a problem.” It’s a fast and easy way to lure people into your copy, and it’s supported by some of the biggest names in advertising. Limit your opening paragraph to a maximum of eleven words. —David Ogilvy Prescription #4: Pile on the Personal Pronoun Personality Finally, I want you to load your copy with pronouns, such as you, me, I, he, she, him, they, and them. Be especially generous with the words you and I. Pronouns give your copy a warm, human flavor that people notice instantly. It helps turn your mass communication into personal communication, the most effective kind. In fact, It’s nearly impossible to overuse the word you in well-written copy. Generously sprinkle it throughout like shaking parmesan cheese on a pizza. Start sentences with it! End sentences with it! Blow it up in big type! Put it in your headline! Ask questions and make statements using pronouns: “Do you...Can you...Would you...Should you...May I ask you a question? May I ask your advice? Can I get your opinion? Did you know...Let me tell you...I think you’ll like this idea...” Ad-Agency Secrets 89 Okay, let’s review what you learned so far. YOU LEARNED that in order for your advertising to be successful, you must first be aware of what blocks your readers from understanding your message. YOU LEARNED that your readers don’t care about your big vocabulary, only what you can do for them. That means you use shorter words, sentences, and paragraphs. YOU LEARNED that advertising copy doesn’t have to follow all the rules of a college composition. Your copy has one job: to sell, Sell, SELL! YOU LEARNED how to use questions to draw people into your copy and keep them reading. Right? YOU LEARNED how to use pronouns, such as the words you and I to make your copy sound personal. And you now know an easy way to determine the readability of your copy by using the Flesch formula. CA$HVERTISING Tip: Do you see how I kept repeating the words you learned in the five preceding paragraphs? Paragraph leaders are a powerful way to increase reading speed and establish an upbeat tempo in your ads. The repetition increases the reader’s perception of volume, and, according the Length-Implies-Strength heuristic discussed in Chapter 2—can help boost credibility. Other effective paragraph leaders are, “We Guarantee...,” “We Promise...,” “You’ll Receive...,” and similar. And even if you really didn’t learn all those things (despite my parroting “you learned”), the mere repetition of the word can cause you to doubt your own feelings because “it’s so confident...it’s so specific...and there are so many of them.” Ad-Agency Secret #2: Bombard Your Readers With Benefits Let’s now talk about the million-dollar secret for getting inside your readers’ heads: benefits. Play close attention. If you don’t incorporate this idea in all of your advertising, you may as well pack up now and try a different business that sells to beings other than humans. Remember our discussion about the Life-Force 8 from Chapter 1? As you may recall, the LF8 are the primary human desires that are hardwired into our brains. These are powerful wants we’re biologically driven to fulfill, no matter who we are, where we live, or what we do. If your product or service can satisfy one of these desires—or any of the nine CA$HVERTISING 90 secondary wants—you have the making of killer benefit claims that can start the sales ball rolling. The fact is, if you don’t put benefits in your advertising, whether it’s an ad, brochure, sales letter, Website, or whatever, then kiss your money goodbye! Now, before you start puckering up, let’s examine what a benefit is, in advertising terms. Benefits are those things that offer your prospects value. And as the word implies, they’re things that directly benefit not you, but your prospect. Is a benefit the same as a feature? No! You must learn the distinction. A feature is simply a component of a product or service. For example: PRODUCT: PRODUCT: Rolls-Royce Phantom Coupé FEATURE: FEATURE: Top-grade, hand-selected seat leathers. BENEFIT: BENEFIT: Luxurious BENEFIT: comfort in all climates. FEATURE: FEATURE: Deep-pile Wilton lamb’s wool carpeting. BENEFIT: BENEFIT: The BENEFIT: rich softness underfoot and lush elegance. FEATURE: FEATURE: 453 FEATURE: horsepower, 6.75-liter V-12 engine. BENEFIT: BENEFIT: Power, BENEFIT: control, supreme reliability. FEATURE: FEATURE: Bold, FEATURE: dignified styling with artist Charles Sykes’s “Spirit of Ecstasy” flying proudly on the hood. BENEFIT: BENEFIT: The BENEFIT: feeling of power, success, and that you’ve “arrived.” Get it? The features are the attributes. The benefits are what you get from those attributes. The benefits are what entice people to buy. Remember, the entire time people are reading your ads, they’re consciously thinking, “WIIFM?”: “What’s In It For Me?” In fact, they can’t turn it off! Over and over and over and over. It’s like a corrupt MP3 file that never stops repeating. By loading your ads with benefits, telling your prospects how and what they gain, how their lives will improve, you’re answering the “WIIFM” they’re continually trying to satisfy. And when you do, their desire for your product increases, and you’re on your way to making a sale. Consumers buy based on what the product will do for them, not on what ingredients it has. —Newspaper Association of America Ad-Agency Secrets 91 In my workshop, I drive the point home with a popular (and often hilarious) two-person interaction called the “Feature-Benefit Exercise.” I pair up participants and ask one to play the role of the seller, and the other the prospect. The seller starts by telling the prospect one feature of his product or service. Then I instruct the prospect to respond with a loud and annoyed “BIG DEAL! What’s in it for me?” And to convey just how worthless it is to state only the product’s features, I instruct the prospect to simultaneously throw her hands in the air and give a look of pure disgust while shouting this. The seller must begin his reply with the words, “You benefit by....” Here’s a typical interaction. Business Owner: Business Owner: “My Business Owner: product is an ink-jet printer. One feature is multiple ink tanks.” Prospect: Prospect: “BIG Prospect: DEAL! What’s in it for me?!” (Arms flailing overhead.) Business Owner: Business Owner: Business Owner: “You benefit by saving big money because you don’t have to replace the entire cartridge when only one ink color runs out.” Prospect: Prospect: “That’s Prospect: nice...I spend a fortune for ink with my current printer. Business Owner: Business Owner: Business Owner: “Feature: 500-sheet tray.” Prospect: Prospect: “BIG Prospect: DEAL! What’s in it for me?!” (Annoyed look of disgust.) Business Owner: Business Owner: “You Business Owner: benefit by not having to fill the paper tray as often. Most other printers hold half as much.” Prospect: Prospect: Prospect: “Sounds like my printer; it’s a pain to keep filling it.” Business Owner: Business Owner: “Feature: Ultra-draft mode button” Prospect: Prospect: “BIG Prospect: DEAL! What’s in it for me?!” Business Owner: Business Owner: “You benefit Business Owner: by saving serious money on ink because the Ultra-Draft mode uses 50 percent less ink than other printers’ ordinary draft mode.” CA$HVERTISING 92 The room usually erupts with laughter as dozens of prospects shout, with annoyed faces and frantic gestures of impatience and dissatisfaction. By the end of the exercise, the sellers know exactly how to sell their product. After all, they’ve been beaten down by prospects who’ve been given the okay to express what prospects are always thinking anyway! Sorry, but people are not interested in your new equipment (only if it benefits them), or that you’re celebrating your 10th anniversary (unless you’re slashing your prices). Likewise, the photos of your staff might be all warm and fuzzy, but until you’ve poured on the benefits, they won’t do a damned thing to make your cash register ring. Pictures of your newborn baby Tabatha? Forget it! Snapshot of your new cat Lu Lu Lemieux? Please! Benefits are what your prospects really care about. Benefits tap into Consumer Psychology Principle #5: The Means-End Chain we covered in Chapter 2, which suggests to always focus on the core benefits and positive end results. Loading your advertising with benefits is the key to all successful advertising. Tell me quick and tell me true, or else, dear friend, the hell with you... Not how this product came to be, But what the damn thing does for me! —Anonymous Ad-Agency Secret #3: Put Your Biggest Benefit in Your Headline Talk about information overload! Estimates say we’re exposed to anywhere from 247 ads per day (Consumer Reports) to more than 3,000 (Newspaper Association of America). If we’re to stand any chance of convincing, persuading, motivating, selling, we must, must, MUST cut through the clutter! The easiest way to do this is to always—without exception—put your biggest benefit in your headline. Unless your headline sells your product, you have wasted 90 percent of your money. —David Ogilvy Ad-Agency Secrets 93 Did you know that 60 percent of all people who read ads typically read headlines and no more? They skim until they “stub their eyeballs” on something that interests them. That means that about 60 percent of those that see your ad read only the first few words. Yikes! Solution: Put the one thing that’s most important to them in the place where they’re most likely to see it: your headline. For example, let’s say you’re writing a headline for your restaurant workshop that teaches waiters and waitresses how to boost their income. DON’T SAY: DON’T SAY: “Attention Food Servers: New Workshop Teaches You the Tricks of the Trade!” DO SAY: “Attention Food Servers: New Workshop Teaches You How to Boost Your Tips by 512%...or Your Money Back!” If you’re an award-winning interior designer specializing in making ordinary houses look like beautiful model homes: DON’T SAY: DON’T SAY: “Louise Taylor Designs Homes of Distinction” Distinction? This claim is too amorphous; it creates no mental movies, and gives your prospects nothing to grasp. Instead: DO SAY: “Award-Winning Interior Designer Louise Taylor Turns Your House Into a Gorgeous Model Home for Less than You Ever Dreamed Possible!” Ahhh...now we have a real idea of what Louise will do. She’s telling us the #1 reason why someone would hire her: to make their house look beautiful. Is your camera shop drowning in rolls of film because everyone’s going digital? DON’T SAY: DON’T SAY: “Capturing the Best Times of Your Life Is Now a Snap!” DO SAY: “GIANT FILM SALE! CA$HVERTISING 94 All Rolls of 35mm Color Film are 25% Off—This Week Only!” Are you a bakery looking to hook customers with your heavenly new “to-die-for” fudge-filled pastry? DON’T SAY: DON’T SAY: “Come In and Sample Our Latest Confectionary Masterpiece!” DO SAY: “Attention Chocolate Lovers: Now Sink Your Teeth Into the 8 1/2-Pound Fudge-Devil Volcano Pie—Absolutely Free!” See the simplicity? Your headline should immediately select the audience you want to hook. By contrast, I saw an ad in a local shopper paper for a lighting supply store that featured the headline, “We’ll Help You Brighten Up Your Life and Save Big!” Ugh, what a waste. Why? Because it does nothing to select its audience. The ad could be for paint, window cleaning, or even antidepressants! Instead, how about the ridiculously simple headline, “Need Lamps?” Think about it. Who would be attracted to a headline that says “Need Lamps?” Someone who needs lamps, of course! The audience, in this case, is perfectly selected. There’s no guessing for whom it’s meant. The headline is the “ticket on the meat.” Use it to flag down readers who are prospects for the kind of product you are advertising. —David Ogilvy Question: Is a longer or shorter headline more effective? Let’s again turn to psychology. Researchers have conducted hundreds of tests to see just how much the average person can effectively “take in,” or pay attention to. The results from all studies are similar. The average Joe or Jane can process a maximum of five to nine numbers (George A. Miller, The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two, 1956) in a “single act of attention.” Ever wonder why phone numbers are seven digits? Bell Telephone wanted to make them long enough to accommodate the most variations, but short enough that people would remember them. Ad-Agency Secrets 95 Word-wise, most people can grasp the meaning of five to six words in a single glance. So does this mean that short headlines get higher readership? Yes. And studies confirm it. That’s because the number of words in a headline affects reading speed, and therefore affects how much of the headline is read. Here’s an example to drive this point home. If you saw the newspaper headline “WAR!” it takes no effort whatsoever to read and process it, does it? As long as you recognize the word, it communicates its meaning instantly. That’s why the readership is so high. Your eyeballs simply have to hit the word, and it’s as good as read. As you add words, you’re moving in the opposite direction of speed, work, ease, and understanding. Take, for example, the headline, “War Was Declared Yesterday by the Blordoni Tribe in the Nation of Kimbootu Against Its Historically More Aggressive Southern Neighbors, the WoopWoops.” It simply takes more time and effort to pore through a longer headline such as this, despite the silly tribal names. It forces you to think more (and we know most people would rather have cavities drilled than do that), and it adds more opportunities to get lost in meaning and boredom. That’s why short headlines get higher readership. Short headlines enjoy higher readership than long headlines. As headlines grow, readership shrinks. —Starch Research But before you grab an ax and start chopping down your headlines like an oak tree, realize that well-written long headlines can be—and often are—remarkably effective. In fact, some long-copy direct-response ads use extremely long headlines that often flow into extremely long subheads, creating a head/sub introduction dozens of words long! A classic study of 2,500 ads appearing in the Saturday Evening Post was conducted from 1939 to 1940 by researcher Harold J. Rudolph. The results show that the shorter the headline, the greater the readership. CA$HVERTISING 96 In this study, the average readership of the shortest headline is about 1/7th better than the longest. We see the biggest drop in headlines with more than 12 words. According to Rudolf, “These findings, obviously, cannot be interpreted as an indication that a headline, to be consistently well read, need to only be short. Headline content is undoubtedly the major element affecting readership.” The flip side? A short headline isn’t necessarily an effective headline. You can struggle just as much writing three words as you would 15, and your ad could still flop. Oh, sure, you’d likely get higher readership with the three-word headline because it takes no effort to read it, but that doesn’t mean you chose the right words. According to David Ogilvy, longer headlines sell more products. “Okay, Drew. Now I’m even more confused!” Alright...let’s simplify: 1. Always put your biggest benefit in your headline. 2. If you can write two equally effective headlines, the shorter one will likely be read by more people, all other variables being the same. For the purposes of practicality, never ignore rule #1, and keep rule #2 in mind to maximize readership when creating your next ad. There, don’t you feel better? 13+ 77.9% How Many Words in the Headline? How Many People Read the Entire Headline?
